Administered in Japanese: item_text/instructions/option_text carry the study's own Japanese wording from S2 Table (Items of DPSS-R-J), and the _translated columns carry the study's own English from S3 Table (Items of DPSS-R). Instrument is the Disgust Propensity and Sensitivity Scale-Revised, Japanese version (DPSS-R-J).

TRANSCRIPTION DEVIATIONS, all disclosed. (1) Two unambiguous misspellings in the S3 English sheet were corrected from the SAME paper's Table 1, which reprints all 16 English items: item 4 'disgustint items' -> 'disgusting items', item 6 'make my stmach turn' -> 'make my stomach turn'. (2) Two further S3-vs-Table-1 wording differences were NOT changed, because neither is an unambiguous typo and S3 is the dedicated item supplement: item 1 S3 'I avoid disgusting things.' vs Table 1 'I avoid disgusting thing.'; item 11 S3 'It scares me when I faint.' vs Table 1 'It scares me when I feel faint.'. (3) The Japanese instruction cell was stripped of a leading ideographic space (U+3000) and two trailing newlines; the English option label 'Some\ntimes' was joined to 'Sometimes'. Nothing else was normalised.

CAVEAT on the study's own English (affects the _translated columns only, not item_text). The two versions are the authors' parallel forms, not word-for-word translations of each other, and they diverge in two visible places. (a) Instructions: the Japanese asks the respondent to circle the applicable number and does not state an item count, while the English says the questionnaire 'consists of 16 statements' and asks for an 'x' in a box. (b) Item 11: the administered Japanese is 'meMAI ga okiru to kowaku naru' (dizziness), while the study's English reads 'It scares me when I faint'. The Japanese is what respondents read and is what ships in item_text; a reader relying on item_text_translated for item 11 gets the study's wording, not a literal gloss of the Japanese. Below the issues-page bar (a study-internal wording difference, not a text-vs-table mismatch), so no public_note.

RIGHTS: no restriction found, so extracted normally under the silence-is-permission rule. The wording IRW copied is from the CC BY 4.0 PLOS ONE deposit's own S2/S3 supplements (Iwasa, Tanaka & Yamada 2016, 10.1371/journal.pone.0164630; 'This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License'). The DPSS-R's author states no bar: the Italian validation (Bottesi et al., PMC5427091) records that 'Dr. van Overveld provided permission to reproduce the items of DPSS-R, confirming that the questionnaire on his website was without any copyright restrictions'. No fee and no redistribution clause was found for the DPSS-R; the ASI block that stopped the sibling table iwasa_2016_asi in batch_053 is specific to the ASI and does not reach this instrument.

The IRW item codes are the S2 Dataset (.s006 XLSX) header strings verbatim, which are a THIRD, slightly different English rendering of the same six stems (e.g. code 21 reads 'I am afraid that the future...' where the appendix reads "I'm afraid that the future...", and code 25 reads 'to people with weaker profiles, I am happy to be doing so well' where the appendix reads 'to people who have weaker profiles, I'm happy I'm doing so well'). Item codes must be read as join keys, not as the administered wording. Likewise the S2 Dataset stores anchors as 'Strongly disagree/Disagree/Rather disagree/Neither agree or disagree/Rather agree/Agree/Strongly agree', a terser English rendering than the appendix's 'I totally disagree'..'I totally agree'; the shipped option_text_translated follows the appendix, and resp 1..7 is the ascending-agreement coding that data/jablonska_2020_instagram.py's LIKERT_MAP applies to those label strings. The questionnaire prints no instruction text for these items - only the part heading 'Part I. Instagram usage.' covering items 1-25 - so instructions and section_prompt are left blank rather than filled with a heading.

It is NOT the Bergen Social Media / Facebook Addiction Scale, which the paper never mentions. data/jablonska_2020_instagram.py splits that single 13-item adaptation by content into two IRW tables: questionnaire items 1-10 (this table) and items 11-13 (jablonska_2020_profile_grooming, the self-expression facet). The 10 live item codes are the S2 Dataset column headers verbatim and match questionnaire items 1-10 one-to-one, so the content is right and only the instrument name needed correcting; `instrument` names the MFIS adaptation. Clean pass. Polish (administered) wording in the base text fields, the study's own English version in the _translated fields, language=Polish. Both come from S3 Appendix, "Questionnaire (in English and Polish)" (10.1371/journal.pone.0229354.s004), whose Part II / Czesc 2 block lists the 10 RSES items in exactly the order of the live item codes 26-35.

Caveat 1 -- the paper carries TWO different English renderings of these items and they are not the same wording. The live `item` codes are the S2 Dataset (.s006) column headers, which are abbreviated paraphrases (e.g. "32. I think I am a valuable person, at least as much as the rest."), while S3's English questionnaire gives the canonical RSES sentence ("I feel that I'm a person of worth, at least on an equal plane with others."). item_text_translated ships the S3 wording, because that is the version presented as the questionnaire; the item code is left exactly as the live data spells it. The two correspond one-to-one and were checked item by item.

Caveat 2 -- the RSES was NOT administered on its canonical 4-point scale. The paper states: "In the original versions, the measures used possessed different Likert scales. And so, HADS and Rosenberg self-esteem scale had a 4-point scale ... To make our questionnaire more clear to respondents, all items were modified by implementing a 7-point Likert scale". Live resp is 1-7, matching. The seven anchors shipped are the questionnaire's own (Calkowicie sie nie zgadzam ... Calkowicie sie zgadzam); the S2 Dataset records the same seven levels under a third English rendering (Strongly disagree/Disagree/Rather disagree/Neither agree or disagree/Rather agree/Agree/Strongly agree), which is what data/jablonska_2020_instagram.py maps to 1-7, so the resp direction is 1=strongly disagree ... 7=strongly agree and the option order is fixed by the script, not inferred.

Caveat 3 -- instructions and section_prompt are deliberately blank. The questionnaire prints no instruction text at all, only part headings; these items sit under "Czesc 2. Moje samopoczucie." ("Part II. Well-being."), a heading shared with the 14 HADS items of jablonska_2020_hads, so it is neither whole-table framing nor a testlet prompt and was not filed as either. correct_response is blank throughout (attitude scale, no key).

Caveat 4 -- data are stored RAW, not reverse-scored: the five negatively worded items (27,30,31,33,34) correlate -0.05 to -0.48 with the five positively worded ones (26,28,29,32,35) and +0.33 to +0.67 among themselves, and their means (2.57-3.99) sit below the positive items' (5.04-5.46) in a general community sample. Anyone scoring the RSES total must reverse those five first.

Rights -- no restriction on the RSES wording could be found or quoted, so under the 2026-09-04 quote test it ships. The wording IRW copied is from the paper's own CC BY 4.0 supporting information (Jablonska & Zajdel 2020, PLOS ONE), not from any instrument rights holder's page. socy.umd.edu (the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale page) returned no response from this environment, so the instrument holder's own terms were not read directly; absence of a retrievable clause is not absence of a clause.
